🚨🚨🚨 Gulf Economies on the brink of Economic Collapse. 

The economic damage across the Gulf in the first 15 days of the Iran war is far larger than most people realize.

The countries hosting U.S. bases or aligned with Washington are absorbing a massive shock across aviation, tourism, energy, and financial markets.

Here is what the first 15 days look like when you break the numbers down:- 

-AVIATION COLLAPSE

• 27,000 flights cancelled across the Middle East since the conflict began

• Major hubs like Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Doha, and Riyadh operating at drastically reduced capacity

• Overflight corridors across the Gulf that normally handle thousands of aircraft daily have fallen to a fraction of normal traffic

• Gulf states earn large revenues from overflight fees, much of which has effectively disappeared during the conflict

-DUBAI TOURISM SHOCK

• Dubai normally receives 52,000–55,000 tourists per day

• In 15 days, that equals roughly 750,000 tourists who never arrived

• 187,000 hotel bookings cancelled across the city

• Tourism activity across major hospitality zones has collapsed close to zero

-AIRPORT ECONOMIC IMPACT

• Dubai International Airport is estimated to be losing roughly $1 million per minute in economic activity disruption

• That translates to roughly $15 billion in losses in 15 days tied to aviation disruption, retail, logistics, and airport-linked services

-REAL ESTATE & CAPITAL FLIGHT

• Dubai real estate prices down 35% in just 15 days amid panic selling

• Property listings rising rapidly as expatriates prepare potential exit strategies

• Many homes already being offered 20–25% below previous market value

-USED CAR MARKET SIGNAL

• Used car sales have surged to roughly 4,000 vehicles per week

• Many cars listed 20–25% below market price

• In expat economies, selling cars is often the first step before leaving the country

-ENERGY & MILITARY COSTS

• Gulf countries have been under continuous drone and missile threats, forcing heavy use of air defense systems

• Air defense interceptors and combat air patrols cost millions per day per country

• Regional oil infrastructure disruptions and security risks are reducing operational efficiency across energy exports

-EXPAT LABOR RISK

• The Gulf economies depend heavily on foreign workers

• Millions of workers from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and the Philippines power tourism, hospitality, and construction sectors.

• If the conflict continues beyond two months, projections suggest 45,000–55,000 job losses per week across the region

-TOTAL ECONOMIC DAMAGE

• Early estimates suggest $100B–$110B in economic losses across Gulf states already

• That includes aviation collapse, tourism losses, air defense costs, property market stress, and financial disruption

And this is just the first 15 days.

If the war drags on for weeks or months, the Gulf economies could face one of the largest regional economic shocks since the early 1990s Gulf War.
